chapter.name: Ray Optics and Optical Instruments
chapter.blurb: The chapter treats light as rays and uses the laws of reflection and refraction, with the Cartesian sign convention, to locate images formed by spherical mirrors, spherical refracting surfaces and thin lenses. It covers total internal reflection and its uses, the lens maker's formula, power and combination of lenses, and refraction through a prism. It ends with the working and magnification of the simple microscope, the compound microscope and refracting and reflecting telescopes.

scope_in.item: State the laws of reflection and apply them at any point of a spherical mirror, taking the normal along the radius; use the terms pole, principal axis, paraxial rays, principal focus and focal plane
State and apply the Cartesian sign convention for distances and heights (measured from the pole or optical centre; along the incident light positive, against it negative; upward heights positive)
Obtain and use f = R/2 for paraxial rays; distinguish real and virtual images; use the convenient rays for locating the image formed by a spherical mirror

Use the mirror equation 1/v + 1/u = 1/f and the magnification m = h'/h = -v/u with signs to find the position, nature and size of images formed by concave and convex mirrors, including a partly covered mirror, an object along the axis and the speed of an image in a convex mirror
State the laws of refraction and Snell's law; use relative refractive index, n12 = 1/n21 and n32 = n31 x n12; distinguish optical density from mass density
Describe refraction through a parallel-sided slab (emergent ray parallel, lateral shift) and use apparent depth = real depth / refractive index for near-normal viewing
Explain total internal reflection and the critical angle, use sin ic = n21 (n12 = 1/sin ic) and the tabulated critical angles, and describe the laser demonstration
Explain the use of total internal reflection in totally reflecting prisms and optical fibres (core and cladding, light pipe, low absorption)
Use n2/v - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R for refraction at a single spherical surface with the sign convention
Explain the two-step image formation by a lens and use the lens maker's formula 1/f = (n21 - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2), including a lens immersed in a liquid
Use the thin lens formula 1/v - 1/u = 1/f and magnification m = v/u for convex and concave lenses, real and virtual objects, and the convenient rays for a lens
Use power P = 1/f in dioptre, 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2 + ..., P = P1 + P2 + ... and m = m1 m2 ... for thin lenses in contact, and successive image formation by separated lenses

Use r1 + r2 = A and delta = i + e - A for a prism; describe the variation of deviation with angle of incidence and the minimum deviation condition; use n21 = sin[(A + Dm)/2]/sin(A/2) and Dm = (n21 - 1)A for a thin prism
Explain the simple microscope and use m = 1 + D/f (image at near point) and m = D/f (image at infinity)
Describe the compound microscope and use mo = L/fo, me = D/fe or 1 + D/fe and m = mo me

Describe the refracting telescope and use m = fo/fe and tube length fo + fe; explain light-gathering power and resolving power in terms of objective diameter; describe the reflecting (Cassegrain) telescope and its advantages

concepts.name: Laws of reflection, the Cartesian sign convention and the focal length of spherical mirrors
concepts.description: The laws of reflection applied to spherical mirrors, the terms pole, principal axis, principal focus and focal plane, the Cartesian sign convention, and the relation between focal length and radius of curvature for paraxial rays.
concepts.idea: A spherical mirror obeys the laws of reflection at every point, with the normal along the radius; one agreed sign convention then lets a single formula handle every mirror and lens case.
concepts.rule: Laws of reflection: the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence, and the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal at the point of incidence lie in one plane; they hold at each point of any reflecting surface, plane or curved. For a spherical mirror the normal at a point is along the radius, the line joining the centre of curvature to the point of incidence. The geometric centre of a spherical mirror is its pole (for a lens, the optical centre); the line joining the pole and the centre of curvature is the principal axis. Cartesian sign convention: all distances are measured from the pole of the mirror or the optical centre of the lens; distances measured in the same direction as the incident light are positive and those measured opposite to it are negative; heights measured upwards, normal to the principal axis, are positive and heights measured downwards are negative. Paraxial rays are incident close to the pole and make small angles with the principal axis. A paraxial beam parallel to the principal axis converges to the principal focus F of a concave mirror, or appears to diverge from F for a convex mirror; a parallel beam inclined at a small angle to the axis converges to (or appears to diverge from) a point in the focal plane, the plane through F normal to the axis. The focal length is the distance between F and the pole, and f = R/2 for paraxial rays (using tan theta approximately equal to theta). f and R are negative for a concave mirror and positive for a convex mirror when the object is in front of the mirror. An image is real if the rays actually converge to the point and virtual if they only appear to diverge from it. Convenient rays: a ray parallel to the axis reflects through (or as if from) the focus; a ray through (or towards) the centre of curvature retraces its path; a ray through (or towards) the focus reflects parallel to the axis; a ray striking the pole reflects obeying the laws of reflection.
concepts.example: A concave mirror of radius of curvature 30 cm has f = R/2 = -15 cm in the Cartesian sign convention, because its focus lies in front of the mirror, against the direction of the incident light.

questions.q: For a concave mirror, a ray parallel to the principal axis strikes the mirror at M and is reflected through the point F on the axis. C is the centre of curvature, P the pole, and D is the foot of the perpendicular from M to the axis. Taking the angle of incidence as theta, obtain the relation between the focal length f and the radius of curvature R for paraxial rays.
questions.a: CM is the normal at M, so the angle of incidence is theta, angle MCP = theta and angle MFP = 2 theta. From the right-angled triangles, tan theta = MD/CD and tan 2theta = MD/FD. For paraxial rays theta is small, so tan theta = theta and tan 2theta = 2 theta, giving MD/FD = 2 MD/CD, that is FD = CD/2. For small theta the point D is very close to P, so FD = f and CD = R. Hence f = R/2.
s: Angle MCP = theta and angle MFP = 2 theta; tan theta = MD/CD and tan 2theta = MD/FD
Small-angle approximation gives FD = CD/2
D is close to P, so FD = f, CD = R and f = R/2

questions.a: They do not. The result that a ray parallel to the axis is reflected through a single point F midway between the pole and the centre of curvature uses the small-angle approximation tan theta = theta, valid only for rays striking close to the pole. Rays that strike far from the pole have large theta, the approximation fails, and they cross the axis at points different from F, so there is no single sharp focus.
s: The single focus relies on the small-angle (paraxial) approximation

questions.q: A point source is placed in front of (a) a concave mirror that throws its image on a screen and (b) a convex mirror. Analyse the difference between the two images in terms of what the reflected rays do, explain what it means to call the image point a point-to-point correspondence with the object, and explain why tracing only two rays is enough to locate the image.
questions.a: (a) The reflected rays actually converge to a point, so the image is real and can be received on a screen. (b) The reflected rays do not meet; they only appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror when produced backwards, so the image is virtual. Calling the image a point-to-point correspondence means every ray that leaves the object point and falls on the mirror passes (or appears to pass) through the same image point after reflection; an infinite number of rays leave the source in all directions. Because all of them go through one image point, the intersection of any two convenient rays is enough to locate it.
s: Concave case - rays actually converge, real image on a screen
Convex case - rays only appear to diverge from a point behind the mirror, virtual image
All rays from the object point pass through the one image point, so any two rays locate it

On a spherical mirror the normal at the point of incidence is taken perpendicular to the tangent to the surface there, that is along the radius from the centre of curvature, and measured from this normal the angle of reflection equals the angle of incidence.
s: Judgement - wrong; the laws hold at every point of any reflecting surface

questions.a: Hold the concave mirror facing the distant object and move a small screen in front of it until a sharp image of the object forms on the screen. Rays from a very distant object are nearly parallel to the axis, so they converge at the principal focus; the distance from the pole of the mirror to the screen is therefore the focal length. The radius of curvature is twice this distance (R = 2f). Both the focus and the centre of curvature lie in front of the mirror, against the direction of the incident light, so f and R are negative.
s: Method - form a sharp image of a distant object on a screen and measure the pole-to-screen distance
Reason - parallel rays converge at the focus, so that distance is f, and R = 2f
Signs - f and R are both negative for a concave mirror

concepts.name: The mirror equation and linear magnification
concepts.description: Using the mirror equation and the magnification formula, with the Cartesian sign convention, to find the position, nature and size of images formed by concave and convex mirrors.
concepts.idea: One equation with signed distances locates the image for every spherical mirror, and the sign and size of the magnification tell whether the image is erect or inverted and enlarged or diminished.
concepts.rule: Mirror equation: 1/v + 1/u = 1/f, where u is the object distance, v the image distance and f the focal length, all with signs from the Cartesian convention (a real object in front of the mirror has negative u; f is negative for a concave mirror and positive for a convex mirror). Linear magnification m = h'/h = -v/u, where h and h' are the object and image heights with sign. Negative v means the image is in front of the mirror (real); positive v means it is behind the mirror (virtual). Negative m means an inverted image, positive m an erect image; |m| greater than 1 means enlarged, less than 1 diminished. Although derived for a real, inverted image formed by a concave mirror, both formulae hold for concave and convex mirrors and for real and virtual images. A concave mirror gives a virtual, erect, enlarged image when the object is between the pole and the focus, and a real, inverted image when the object is beyond the focus (beyond 2f when the object is between f and 2f). A convex mirror always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image between the pole and the focus. Covering part of a mirror still gives the image of the whole object but with lower intensity. An object lying along the axis is not magnified uniformly, because magnification depends on object distance. From the mirror equation v = fu/(u - f).
concepts.example: An object 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of radius of curvature 15 cm: f = -7.5 cm, u = -10 cm, so 1/v = 1/(-7.5) - 1/(-10) gives v = -30 cm and m = -v/u = -3; the image is real, inverted and magnified three times.

The side-view mirror of a parked car is a convex mirror of radius of curvature 4 m. A motorcyclist approaches the car at a constant speed of 10 m/s. questions.a: f = R/2 = +2 m. From the mirror equation, v = fu/(u - f). For u = -18 m: v = (2)(-18)/(-18 - 2) = 36/20 = 1.8 m behind the mirror. One second later u = -18 + 10 = -8 m: v = (2)(-8)/(-8 - 2) = 16/10 = 1.6 m behind the mirror. The image moves 1.8 - 1.6 = 0.2 m in 1 s, so its average speed is 0.2 m/s.

u = -8 m after one second gives v = +1.6 m

questions.q: Using the mirror equation with the Cartesian sign convention, analyse the sign of the image distance for a real object placed at any distance in front of a convex mirror, and say what it shows about where the image lies.
questions.a: For a real object u is negative, and for a convex mirror f is positive. From the mirror equation 1/v = 1/f - 1/u; since u is negative, -1/u is positive, so 1/v is the sum of two positive terms and v is positive whatever the object distance. Positive v means the image lies behind the mirror, so it is always virtual.
s: u negative and f positive give 1/v = 1/f - 1/u as a sum of two positive terms
v is always positive - image behind the mirror, always virtual

questions.q: An object is placed in front of a concave mirror at a distance x from the pole, where x lies between F and 2F (F is the magnitude of the focal length). Using the mirror equation with the Cartesian sign convention, deduce whether the image is real or virtual, how far it is from the mirror compared with 2F, and whether it is enlarged.
questions.a: u = -x and f = -F. Mirror equation: 1/v = 1/f - 1/u = -1/F + 1/x = -(x - F)/(Fx), so v = -Fx/(x - F). Since x is greater than F, v is negative: the image is in front of the mirror and real. Its distance is Fx/(x - F); this exceeds 2F when x is greater than 2(x - F), that is when x is less than 2F, which is true. So the image lies beyond 2F. Magnitude of magnification = |v/u| = F/(x - F), which is greater than 1 because x - F is less than F, so the image is enlarged (and inverted, m being negative).
s: Substitution u = -x, f = -F gives v = -Fx/(x - F), negative, so real
Image distance Fx/(x - F) is greater than 2F because x is less than 2F
|m| = F/(x - F) is greater than 1 - enlarged (inverted)

questions.q: An object is 10 cm in front of a concave mirror whose focal length has magnitude 15 cm. A student substitutes u = +10 cm and f = +15 cm into the mirror equation, obtains v = -30 cm, and concludes that the image is real and 30 cm in front of the mirror. Evaluate the working and the conclusion.

concepts.name: Refraction, Snell's law, refractive index and apparent depth
concepts.description: The laws of refraction, relative refractive index and its properties, optical density, refraction through a parallel-sided slab, and apparent depth for near-normal viewing.
concepts.idea: At an interface light changes direction according to Snell's law, and the relative refractive index of the pair of media fixes how much it bends.
concepts.rule: Refraction is the change in direction of propagation of an obliquely incident ray (0 < i < 90 degrees) on entering another transparent medium. Laws of refraction: (i) the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the interface at the point of incidence lie in the same plane; (ii) sin i / sin r = n21, a constant called the refractive index of medium 2 with respect to medium 1 (Snell's law), where i and r are measured from the normal. n21 is a characteristic of the pair of media and depends on the wavelength of light, but is independent of the angle of incidence. If n21 > 1 then r < i: the ray bends towards the normal and medium 2 is optically denser than medium 1. If n21 < 1 then r > i: the ray bends away from the normal (denser to rarer). Optical density is not mass density: turpentine has lower mass density than water but is optically denser. n12 = 1/n21, and n32 = n31 x n12. For a parallel-sided slab the emergent ray is parallel to the incident ray (no deviation) but suffers a lateral shift. The bottom of a tank of water appears raised: for viewing near the normal, apparent depth = real depth / refractive index of the medium.
concepts.example: A needle at the bottom of a tank filled with water to a height of 12.5 cm appears at a depth of 9.4 cm, so the refractive index of water is 12.5/9.4 = 1.33.

concepts.name: Total internal reflection, the critical angle and its applications
concepts.description: The conditions for total internal reflection, the critical angle and its relation to refractive index, and the use of total internal reflection in prisms and optical fibres.
concepts.idea: Light going from a denser to a rarer medium is completely reflected back once the angle of incidence exceeds the critical angle, because Snell's law can no longer be satisfied.
concepts.rule: When light travels from an optically denser to a rarer medium it is partly reflected back (internal reflection) and partly refracted, bending away from the normal. As the angle of incidence increases so does the angle of refraction, until it reaches 90 degrees and the refracted ray grazes the interface; the angle of incidence for which r = 90 degrees is the critical angle ic for that pair of media. For i greater than ic no refraction is possible (Snell's law would need sin r greater than 1) and the ray is totally reflected: total internal reflection. In ordinary reflection some light is always transmitted, so the reflected ray is less intense than the incident ray; in total internal reflection no light is transmitted. sin ic = n21 (rarer medium 2 with respect to denser medium 1), so the refractive index of the denser medium with respect to the rarer is n12 = 1/sin ic. Critical angles with respect to air: water (n = 1.33) 48.75 degrees, crown glass (1.52) 41.14 degrees, dense flint glass (1.62) 37.31 degrees, diamond (2.42) 24.41 degrees. Applications: prisms that bend light by 90 degrees or 180 degrees, or invert an image without changing its size, need ic less than 45 degrees; optical fibres have a core of higher refractive index than the cladding, so light undergoes repeated total internal reflections along the fibre with no appreciable loss, even if the fibre is bent; fibres carry audio and video signals and act as a light pipe for examining internal organs; the main requirement is very little absorption of light in the fibre material.
concepts.example: For diamond (n = 2.42) sin ic = 1/2.42, giving ic = 24.41 degrees, so a ray inside diamond meeting the surface at 30 degrees is totally reflected.

concepts.name: Refraction at a spherical surface and the lens maker's formula
concepts.description: Image formation by a single spherical refracting surface, and the lens maker's formula obtained by applying it at the two surfaces of a thin lens, including a lens immersed in a liquid.
concepts.idea: A lens is two spherical refracting surfaces back to back: applying the single-surface relation twice, with the first image as the object for the second surface, gives the focal length in terms of the radii and the refractive indices.
concepts.rule: For refraction at a spherical surface from a medium of refractive index n1 (the side from which light is incident) to a medium of refractive index n2: n2/v - n1/u = (n2 - n1)/R, with u, v and R measured from the pole of the surface with the Cartesian sign convention (R is positive when the centre of curvature lies on the side towards which the light is travelling). The normal at the point of incidence passes through the centre of curvature; the aperture is assumed small so that small-angle approximations hold (n1 i = n2 r). The relation holds for any curved spherical surface. A thin lens is a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one of which is spherical. The first surface forms an image that acts as a (virtual) object for the second surface. The focus is the point where the image of an object at infinity is formed, and its distance from the lens is the focal length. Lens maker's formula: 1/f = (n21 - 1)(1/R1 - 1/R2), where n21 = n2/n1 is the refractive index of the lens material with respect to the surrounding medium and R1, R2 are the signed radii of the first and second surfaces. For a double convex lens R1 is positive and R2 negative, giving positive f; for a double concave lens R1 is negative and R2 positive, giving negative f. A lens immersed in a liquid of the same refractive index has 1/f = 0: it acts like a plane sheet and disappears from view.
concepts.example: A double convex lens with radii of curvature 10 cm and 15 cm and focal length 12 cm: 1/12 = (n - 1)(1/10 + 1/15), which gives n = 1.5.

concepts.name: The thin lens formula, magnification, power of a lens and lenses in contact
concepts.description: Locating and describing images formed by convex and concave lenses with the thin lens formula, the magnification of a lens, the power of a lens in dioptres, and combinations of thin lenses.
concepts.idea: A single signed formula gives the image for every thin lens, power measures how strongly a lens converges or diverges light, and for thin lenses in contact the powers simply add.
concepts.rule: Thin lens formula: 1/v - 1/u = 1/f, with u, v and f measured from the optical centre using the Cartesian sign convention; f is positive for a converging (convex) lens and negative for a diverging (concave) lens. It holds for convex and concave lenses and for real and virtual images. The two foci of a double convex or double concave lens are equidistant from the optical centre. Convenient rays: a ray parallel to the principal axis passes through the second principal focus of a convex lens (or appears to diverge from the first principal focus of a concave lens); a ray through the optical centre emerges undeviated; a ray through the first principal focus of a convex lens (or heading towards the second focus of a concave lens) emerges parallel to the axis. Magnification m = h'/h = v/u: m is positive for an erect (virtual) image and negative for an inverted (real) image. Power P = 1/f with f in metres; the SI unit is the dioptre (1 D = 1 m^-1); P is positive for a converging lens and negative for a diverging lens; a shorter focal length bends light more. For thin lenses in contact, 1/f = 1/f1 + 1/f2 + ... and P = P1 + P2 + ... (algebraic sum); the total magnification is the product m = m1 m2 m3 .... For lenses not in contact, the image formed by one lens serves as the object for the next; an image that would form beyond the next lens acts as a virtual object for it (positive u).
concepts.example: A lens of focal length 0.5 m has power 1/0.5 = +2 D.

concepts.name: Refraction through a prism and the angle of minimum deviation
concepts.description: The passage of a ray through a triangular prism, the angle of deviation and its dependence on the angle of incidence, the condition of minimum deviation, the prism formula for refractive index, and the thin prism.
concepts.idea: A prism deviates a ray by an amount that depends on the angle of incidence and is least when the ray passes symmetrically; measuring that minimum deviation gives the refractive index.
concepts.rule: For a triangular prism of angle A, a ray is incident on the first face at angle i and refracted at r1, meets the second face from inside at r2 and emerges at angle e. Geometry gives r1 + r2 = A. The angle of deviation delta is the angle between the emergent ray and the direction of the incident ray: delta = (i - r1) + (e - r2) = i + e - A. The deviation depends on the angle of incidence; plotted against i it first decreases, reaches a minimum Dm and then increases. Any value of delta other than the minimum corresponds to two angles of incidence, because delta is unchanged when i and e are interchanged (the path of the ray can be traced back). At minimum deviation i = e, so r1 = r2 = A/2, the refracted ray inside the prism is parallel to its base, and Dm = 2i - A, that is i = (A + Dm)/2. The refractive index of the prism material with respect to the surrounding medium is n21 = sin[(A + Dm)/2] / sin(A/2); measuring A and Dm therefore gives the refractive index. For a thin (small-angle) prism Dm = (n21 - 1)A, so thin prisms do not deviate light much.
concepts.example: A thin prism of angle 4 degrees and refractive index 1.5 deviates light by (1.5 - 1) x 4 = 2 degrees.

concepts.description: How a single converging lens acts as a magnifier, its magnification for the image at the near point and at infinity, and the construction, image formation and magnification of a compound microscope.
concepts.idea: A magnifier lets the object be brought closer to the eye than the near point so that it subtends a larger angle; a compound microscope multiplies the magnification of an objective by that of an eyepiece.
concepts.rule: A simple microscope (magnifier) is a converging lens of small focal length held near the object, one focal length away or less, with the eye close to the lens; it gives an erect, magnified, virtual image. With the image at the near point (D = 25 cm, the least distance of distinct vision) the magnification is m = 1 + D/f; with the image at infinity (object at the focus, relaxed eye) the angular magnification is m = D/f, one less, but viewing is more comfortable. The magnifier works by letting the object be brought closer to the eye than D. A simple microscope has a limited maximum magnification (about 9 or less) for realistic focal lengths. A compound microscope uses two lenses: the objective, nearest the object, forms a real, inverted, magnified image; this lies at or just within the focal plane of the eyepiece, which acts as a simple magnifier and gives an enlarged, virtual final image that is inverted with respect to the object. Magnification of the objective mo = h'/h = L/fo, where the tube length L is the distance between the second focal point of the objective and the first focal point of the eyepiece. Eyepiece: me = 1 + D/fe (final image at the near point) or me = D/fe (final image at infinity). Total magnification m = mo me = (L/fo)(D/fe) for the final image at infinity. Both the objective and the eyepiece should have short focal lengths for large magnification.
concepts.example: With fo = 1.0 cm, fe = 2.0 cm and tube length 20 cm, m = (20/1)(25/2) = 250.

questions.a: Without the lens, the object cannot be seen clearly if it is closer than the near point D (25 cm), so the largest angle it can subtend is that when it is at D. With the lens the object can be placed much closer to the eye than D, at about the focal length, while its image is formed at a distance where the eye can see it comfortably. The angle subtended is therefore larger than the angle the object would subtend at D, and the ratio of these two angles is the angular magnification.

Lens formula gives u = -2.5 cm (object 2.5 cm from the objective); mo = -4

Tube length L = mo fo = 7.5 cm
Separation of the lenses = fo + L + fe = 13.75 cm

concepts.name: Telescopes: refracting and reflecting
concepts.description: The refracting telescope and its magnifying power and tube length, the importance of a large objective, and the reflecting (Cassegrain) telescope and its advantages.
concepts.idea: A telescope gives angular magnification of a distant object using a long-focus, wide objective and a short-focus eyepiece; large modern telescopes replace the objective lens with a concave mirror.
concepts.rule: A telescope provides angular magnification of distant objects. It has an objective of large focal length and much larger aperture than the eyepiece. Light from a distant object forms a real image at the second focal point of the objective; the eyepiece magnifies this image, giving a final inverted image. Magnifying power m = beta/alpha, the ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the final image to the angle the object subtends at the lens or the eye; m = fo/fe, and the length of the telescope tube is fo + fe (final image at infinity). The image formed by the objective has height h = fo x alpha (alpha in radian). Terrestrial telescopes have, in addition, a pair of inverting lenses to make the final image erect. The main considerations for an astronomical telescope are its light-gathering power, which depends on the area of the objective, and its resolving power (the ability to observe distinctly two objects in very nearly the same direction), which also depends on the diameter of the objective; so objectives of large diameter are desired. Large lenses are heavy, hard to make and to support by their edges, and expensive to make free of chromatic aberration and distortions. Reflecting telescopes use a concave mirror as the objective: a mirror has no chromatic aberration, weighs much less than a lens of equivalent optical quality and can be supported over its entire back surface. The objective mirror focusses light inside the tube; in a Cassegrain telescope a convex secondary mirror reflects the light back through a hole in the primary mirror to the eyepiece, giving a large focal length in a short telescope.
concepts.example: A telescope with an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 1 cm has magnifying power 100/1 = 100; two stars 1 minute of arc apart appear 100 minutes of arc (1.67 degrees) apart.

questions.q: Both a compound microscope and a refracting telescope have an objective and an eyepiece. Compare the focal length chosen for the objective in the two instruments and explain the difference from how each instrument magnifies.
questions.a: In a compound microscope the objective has a short focal length, because the magnification produced by the objective is the tube length divided by its focal length, so a smaller focal length gives a larger magnification. In a telescope the objective has a large focal length (and a large aperture), because its magnifying power is the focal length of the objective divided by that of the eyepiece, so a longer objective focal length gives a larger magnifying power.
s: Microscope objective - short focal length, since its magnification varies inversely with fo
Telescope objective - long focal length, since the magnifying power is fo/fe

questions.q: Analyse why astronomers aim to build telescopes with objectives of the largest possible diameter, and why this aim leads to mirrors rather than lenses being used as objectives.
questions.a: A larger objective has a larger area and so a greater light-gathering power, allowing fainter objects to be observed. The resolving power, the ability to observe distinctly two objects in very nearly the same direction, also depends on the diameter of the objective. But very large lenses are heavy, hard to make and to support by their edges, and difficult and expensive to make free of chromatic aberration and distortions. A mirror has no chromatic aberration, weighs much less than a lens of equivalent optical quality, and can be supported over its whole back surface, so large objectives are made as concave mirrors.
s: Light-gathering power depends on the area of the objective - fainter objects seen
Resolving power also depends on the diameter of the objective
Large lenses are heavy and hard to support and correct; mirrors avoid these problems

questions.a: The reasoning is wrong. The magnifying power of a telescope is fo/fe, so a shorter objective focal length would reduce it. To increase the magnifying power the objective should have a longer focal length, or the eyepiece a shorter one.
s: Magnifying power of a telescope is fo/fe, so a shorter fo reduces it

questions.a: Magnifying power = fo/fe must be 40. The possible long-focus objectives are P and Q: P with S gives 200/5 = 40, P with T gives 100, Q with S gives 10 and Q with T gives 25. So the objective is P (focal length 200 cm) and the eyepiece is S (focal length 5 cm). P is suitable as the objective because it has the large focal length and the large aperture needed to gather light. Tube length = fo + fe = 200 + 5 = 205 cm.

Choice - P (200 cm, large aperture) as objective and S (5 cm) as eyepiece
Tube length = fo + fe = 205 cm
